stemBlocks.value: Solve the simultaneous equations x − y = 3 and x² − y² = 21.
Think first: Notice that x² − y² is a difference of two squares — factorising it makes this almost immediate.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p112-q09 from workbook page 112.

solutionSteps.instruction: Factorise the second equation as a difference of two squares.
Substitute x − y = 3 from the first equation.
Add this to x − y = 3 to eliminate y.
Substitute back to find y, then check.

strategyBlocks.value: Factorise x² − y² as (x − y)(x + y), substitute the known value of x − y to find x + y, then solve the two linear equations together.

whyThisWorks.value: Recognising the difference of two squares turns the non-linear equation into a product in which one factor is already known, so it collapses into a second linear equation. From there the system is an ordinary pair of linear simultaneous equations solved by elimination. Substituting and expanding would also work but takes considerably longer.

commonErrors.misconception: Writing x² − y² as (x − y)² and losing the second factor.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Writing x² − y² as (x − y)² and losing the second factor.

commonErrors.misconception: Dividing 21 by 3 but calling the result x rather than x + y.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Dividing 21 by 3 but calling the result x rather than x + y.

commonErrors.misconception: Subtracting the two linear equations when adding is what eliminates y.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Subtracting the two linear equations when adding is what eliminates y.

examTip.value: Whenever x² − y² appears in a simultaneous-equation question, factorise it first — the other equation almost always supplies one of the brackets.
